newsitem.title: CHINA: China doctors get hand from Harvard, technology.
newsitem.headline: China doctors get hand from Harvard, technology.

text.p: China gained a glimpse of the medical future on Friday when a video link enabled a team of Harvard doctors to help treat a Chinese boy with a rare disease.

As U.S. Ambassador James Sasser and China's health minister Chen Minzhang looked on, doctors from Harvard-affiliated hospitals in Boston and Peking (Beijing) Union Medical College used telemedicine to analyse the case of a five-year-old boy with the rare fungal infection cryptococcosis.

The boy, whose name was not made public, may have contracted the disease from pigeons that his family raised near their home in a fishing village in eastern China's Shandong province, Chinese doctors said.
Doctors from Brigham and Women's Hospital and Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston took part in the video conference.
"This was the first such case in China," said Dr Wang Aixia, chief of the Beijing hospital's section for treating infectious diseases.
"Chinese doctors diagnosed the disease but getting treatment recommendations this way was very useful," she said.
Chinese doctors said the boy, who had a fever and swollen lymph nodes, was responding to treatment.
While the use of high-speed telephone lines for video conferences in medical and other fields is common in developed countries, it has so far seen little use in China.
China is anxious to upgrade medical treatment for its 1.2 billion people but it is short of resources needed for expensive medecines and technology.
The cost of such high-speed connections for a video conference could be prohibitive for most Chinese hospitals.
In addition to the cost of the equipment itself, a one- minute link between China and the United States, billed from Beijing, would be $50, thereby limiting widespread use of the technology.
In this case, American companies helped with the costs.
